claim: Dopaminergic neurons displayed a 42.1% (+/−1.4%) loss in fluorescence signal intensity within 24 hr after injury in C. elegans.
source: When compared to age-matched non-injured counterparts, dopaminergic neurons displayed the greatest reduction in fluorescence with a 42.1% (+/−1.4%) loss in signal intensity within 24 hr after injury, indicative of elevated sensitivity to degeneration (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from large-particle flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 1A, with specific quantitative values and error margins provided.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons in C. elegans show fluorescence beading in dendritic processes 24 hr after injury.
source: Microscopic examination of dopaminergic neurons revealed phenotypes characteristic of neuronal damage (Gennarelli, 1996; Kilinc et al., 2009) 24 hr after injury, including fluorescence beading in dendritic processes (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopic imaging data shown in Figure 1B and cited references to established neuronal damage phenotypes.

claim: Fluorescence beading in dendritic processes is characteristic of neuronal damage.
source: Microscopic examination of dopaminergic neurons revealed phenotypes characteristic of neuronal damage (Gennarelli, 1996; Kilinc et al., 2009) 24 hr after injury, including fluorescence beading in dendritic processes (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to established literature on neuronal damage phenotypes.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra exhibited increased apoptosis seven days after concussive injury in mice.
source: Seven days after injury, dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra exhibited signs of increased apoptosis as evidenced by enhanced immunofluorescence staining of cleaved caspase-3, and a 59.06% (+/−3.03%) loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons was observed 28 days post-trauma (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing cleaved caspase-3 staining in Figure 1C and D.

claim: A 59.06% (+/−3.03%) loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons was observed 28 days post-trauma in mice.
source: Seven days after injury, dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra exhibited signs of increased apoptosis as evidenced by enhanced immunofluorescence staining of cleaved caspase-3, and a 59.06% (+/−3.03%) loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons was observed 28 days post-trauma (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from immunofluorescence measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Closed-head brain injury without cranial fracture revealed no significant cleaved caspase-3 staining in the hippocampus, thalamus and visual cortex seven days post-injury.
source: Yet, one study demonstrates neuronal loss within the substantia nigra (Liu et al., 2017). In contrast, closed-head brain injury without cranial fracture revealed no significant cleaved caspase-3 staining in the hippocampus, thalamus and visual cortex seven days post-injury (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–I.

claim: Neuroinflammation was not evident in the immunolabeling of microglia (IBA1) with CD68-positive inflammatory cytoplasmic granules after closed-head injury.
source: Furthermore, neuroinflammation was not evident in the immunolabeling of microglia (IBA1) with CD68-positive inflammatory cytoplasmic granules or in the transcriptional activation of known inflammatory targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–K.

claim: Transcriptional activation of known inflammatory targets was not evident after closed-head injury.
source: Furthermore, neuroinflammation was not evident in the immunolabeling of microglia (IBA1) with CD68-positive inflammatory cytoplasmic granules or in the transcriptional activation of known inflammatory targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J–K.

claim: Concussed mice showed reduced latency on the accelerating rotarod coincident with dopaminergic degeneration.
source: In concussed mice, we observed reduced latency on the accelerating rotarod and decreased resting state ambulation coincident with dopaminergic degeneration (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from rotarod testing shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Concussed mice showed decreased resting state ambulation coincident with dopaminergic degeneration.
source: In concussed mice, we observed reduced latency on the accelerating rotarod and decreased resting state ambulation coincident with dopaminergic degeneration (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ambulation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons within the midbrain comprise the nigrostriatal circuit, which influences voluntary movement.
source: Dopaminergic neurons within the midbrain comprise the nigrostriatal circuit, which influences voluntary movement.
evidence: The claim is based on established neuroscience knowledge about the nigrostriatal circuit.

claim: Modeling blunt force trauma in C. elegans and concussive injury in mice demonstrate conserved hypersensitivity of dopaminergic neurons to biomechanical insult.
source: Thus, modeling blunt force trauma in C. elegans and concussive injury in mice demonstrate conserved hypersensitivity of dopaminergic neurons to biomechanical insult.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental data in both C. elegans and mice models.

claim: A peak effective stress of 22.8 kPa (corresponding principal strain of 8.3%) first appeared in the cortex region at 0.31 ms after impact.
source: By FEM analysis, a peak effective stress of 22.8 kPa (corresponding principal strain of 8.3%) first appeared in the cortex region at 0.31 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by finite element model analysis data.

claim: Stress propagated to 28.62 kPa (corresponding principal strain of 23.6% at the thalamus and 18.5% at the substantia nigra) at 0.85 ms post-injury in the thalamus and substantia nigra region.
source: Then, stress propagated to 28.62 kPa (corresponding principal strain of 23.6% at the thalamus and 18.5% at the substantia nigra) at 0.85 ms post-injury in the thalamus and substantia nigra region.
evidence: The claim is supported by finite element model analysis data.

claim: A stress wave caused another peak effective stress of around 30 kPa (corresponding principal strain of 40.9% at the brainstem region and 27.0% at the thalamus region) at 1.64 ms after impacting.
source: After impacting, a stress wave caused another peak effective stress of around 30 kPa (corresponding principal strain of 40.9% at the brainstem region and 27.0% at the thalamus region) at 1.64 ms (Figure 2A–C; Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by finite element model analysis data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons may be sensitized to biomechanical insults due to inherent physiological properties since non-invasive, linear impact generates a strain within the midbrain comparable to brain regions closer to the impact site that lack evidence of neuronal death.
source: Thus, dopaminergic neurons may be sensitized to biomechanical insults due to inherent physiological properties since non-invasive, linear impact generates a strain within the midbrain comparable to brain regions closer to the impact site that lack evidence of neuronal death.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the finite element model data and the observation of selective dopaminergic neurodegeneration.

claim: Traumatic brain injury with a loss of consciousness presents a significant risk factor for development of Parkinson's disease (PD), Parkinsonism, and Lewy body accumulation.
source: Longitudinal studies from the clinic show that traumatic brain injury with a loss of consciousness presents a significant risk factor for development of Parkinson's disease (PD), Parkinsonism, and Lewy body accumulation (Crane et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to longitudinal clinical studies.

claim: The pathology and motor deficits observed after concussive injury in mice are similar to those of individuals with PD.
source: Indeed, the pathology and motor deficits that we observed after concussive injury in mice are similar to those of individuals with PD.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison of experimental observations with known PD characteristics.

claim: Mitochondrial components including the electron transport chain (ETC) have emerged as prominent drivers of PD based on familial links and environmental risk factors.
source: Based on familial links and environmental risk factors, mitochondrial components including the electron transport chain (ETC) have emerged as prominent drivers of PD (Perier and Vila, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on PD mechanisms.

claim: Reducing the complex IV cytochrome C oxidase activity of the ETC through cox-5b RNAi promotes a dose-dependent survival of dopaminergic neurons after injury in C. elegans.
source: Utilizing our C. elegans trauma model, we found that reducing the complex IV cytochrome C oxidase activity of the ETC through cox-5b RNAi promotes a dose-dependent survival of dopaminergic neurons after injury (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Reduced expression of cox-5b exclusively in the nervous system was sufficient to promote survival of dopaminergic neurons after blunt force trauma.
source: Moreover, reduced expression of cox-5b exclusively in the nervous system was sufficient to promote survival of dopaminergic neurons after blunt force trauma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tissue-specific RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Surf1 mutations reduce rather than ablate cytochrome C oxidase activity, leading to a 53.9% reduction in function.
source: Surf1 mutations reduce rather than ablate cytochrome C oxidase activity, leading to a 53.9% reduction in function (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring cytochrome C oxidase activity shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Surf1-/- mice exhibited a 40% reduction in mortality rate following lethal head trauma compared to wild type littermates.
source: Surf1-/- mice exhibited a 40% reduction in mortality rate following lethal head trauma and a 2.3-fold improvement in post-injury reflex recovery time compared to wild type littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting immediate protection against TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on mortality rates shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Surf1-/- mice showed a 2.3-fold improvement in post-injury reflex recovery time compared to wild type littermates.
source: Surf1-/- mice exhibited a 40% reduction in mortality rate following lethal head trauma and a 2.3-fold improvement in post-injury reflex recovery time compared to wild type littermates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D), suggesting immediate protection against TBI.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on reflex recovery shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cleaved caspase-3 signal intensity within the midbrain was reduced by 55% (+/−3.5%) after 7 days in concussed Surf1-/- mice.
source: Cleaved caspase-3 signal intensity within the midbrain was reduced by 55% (+/−3.5%) after 7 days in concussed Surf1-/- mice (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Surf1-/- mice showed increased latency in high-speed rotarod analysis compared to wild-type littermates after concussion.
source: Coincident with decreased neurodegeneration, Surf1-/-mice showed increased latency in high-speed rotarod analysis compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 3E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from rotarod testing shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Surf1-/- mice showed a 25.93% (+/−6.828%) dopaminergic loss 28 days post-injury, compared to the 59.06% (+/−3.03%) observed in wild-type counterparts.
source: This was accompanied by a 25.93% (+/−6.828%) dopaminergic loss 28 days post-injury, compared to the 59.06% (+/−3.03%) observed in wild-type counterparts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from neuron counting shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H.

claim: Resting state ambulation was unaffected by trauma in Surf1-/- mice unlike deficits observed in wild-type littermates.
source: Moreover, resting state ambulation was unaffected by trauma in Surf1-/- mice unlike deficits observed in wild-type littermates (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ambulation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Suppressing trauma-induced degeneration of dopaminergic neurons by reduced cytochrome C oxidase activity is evolutionarily conserved between C. elegans and mice.
source: Thus, suppressing trauma-induced degeneration of dopaminergic neurons by reduced cytochrome C oxidase activity is evolutionarily conserved between C. elegans and mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental data in both C. elegans and mice models.

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are toxic by-products of brain injury.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are toxic by-products of brain injury (Hall and Braughler, 1993) that originate in the mitochondrial inner membrane by partial reduction of oxygen.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on brain injury mechanisms.

claim: ROS originate in the mitochondrial inner membrane by partial reduction of oxygen.
source: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are toxic by-products of brain injury (Hall and Braughler, 1993) that originate in the mitochondrial inner membrane by partial reduction of oxygen.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial biochemistry.

claim: Upon accumulation, ROS initiate cellular damage and stress.
source: Upon accumulation, ROS initiate cellular damage and stress.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ROS toxicity.

claim: In genetic and pharmacological models of Parkinson's disease, mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS accumulation underlie dopaminergic neurodegeneration and subsequent disease progression.
source: In genetic and pharmacological models of Parkinson's disease, mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS accumulation underlie dopaminergic neurodegeneration and subsequent disease progression (Blesa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on Parkinson's disease models.

claim: A five fold increase in ROS production was observed immediately after blunt force trauma in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, we observed a five fold increase in ROS production immediately after blunt force trauma, which was suppressed upon cox-5b RNAi (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring ROS production shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ROS production after blunt force trauma was suppressed upon cox-5b RNAi in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, we observed a five fold increase in ROS production immediately after blunt force trauma, which was suppressed upon cox-5b RNAi (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring ROS production shown in Figure 4A.

claim: cox-5b RNAi treatments in C. elegans are reported to reduce oxygen consumption.
source: Since cox-5b RNAi treatments in C. elegans are reported to reduce oxygen consumption (Kaufman and Crowder, 2015), we hypothesized that reduced reliance on mitochondrial respiration mitigates the likelihood of overwhelming respiratory output.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on cox-5b RNAi effects.

claim: Reduced reliance on mitochondrial respiration mitigates the likelihood of overwhelming respiratory output.
source: Since cox-5b RNAi treatments in C. elegans are reported to reduce oxygen consumption (Kaufman and Crowder, 2015), we hypothesized that reduced reliance on mitochondrial respiration mitigates the likelihood of overwhelming respiratory output.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on inference from cited literature.

claim: Reducing the rate of electron transfer between ETC complexes reduces the rate of ROS generation and accumulation.
source: Essentially, reducing the rate of electron transfer between ETC complexes reduces the rate of ROS generation and accumulation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of mitochondrial electron transport and ROS generation.

claim: Elevating neuronal ROS via expression of the mitochondrial targeted oxidative photosensitizer, Tom20::KillerRed, was sufficient to induce dopaminergic neurodegeneration in worms.
source: Indeed, elevating neuronal ROS via expression of the mitochondrial targeted oxidative photosensitizer, Tom20::KillerRed (Wojtovich and Foster, 2014), was sufficient to induce dopaminergic neurodegeneration in worms that could not be suppressed by cox-5b RNAi (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using KillerRed expression shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Dopaminergic neurodegeneration induced by ectopic ROS expression could not be suppressed by cox-5b RNAi.
source: Indeed, elevating neuronal ROS via expression of the mitochondrial targeted oxidative photosensitizer, Tom20::KillerRed (Wojtovich and Foster, 2014), was sufficient to induce dopaminergic neurodegeneration in worms that could not be suppressed by cox-5b RNAi (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using KillerRed expression shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Intra-neuronal ROS production is sufficient to drive dopaminergic degeneration.
source: Thus, intra-neuronal ROS production is sufficient to drive dopaminergic degeneration, while neuroprotection conferred by reduced cytochrome C oxidase activity appears to act upstream of this ROS-induced neurotoxicity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the KillerRed experimental data.

claim: Neuroprotection conferred by reduced cytochrome C oxidase activity appears to act upstream of ROS-induced neurotoxicity.
source: Thus, intra-neuronal ROS production is sufficient to drive dopaminergic degeneration, while neuroprotection conferred by reduced cytochrome C oxidase activity appears to act upstream of this ROS-induced neurotoxicity.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing cox-5b RNAi cannot suppress KillerRed-induced degeneration.

claim: Surf1-/- cells consumed two fold less oxygen than Surf1+/+ cells.
source: Despite no significant change in mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), Surf1-/- cells consumed two fold less oxygen and exhibited reduced reticular mitochondrial morphology (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), strongly suggesting reductions in oxidative phosphorylation (Galloway et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Surf1-/- cells exhibited reduced reticular mitochondrial morphology.
source: Despite no significant change in mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), Surf1-/- cells consumed two fold less oxygen and exhibited reduced reticular mitochondrial morphology (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), strongly suggesting reductions in oxidative phosphorylation (Galloway et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reduced oxygen consumption and reduced reticular mitochondrial morphology strongly suggest reductions in oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Despite no significant change in mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), Surf1-/- cells consumed two fold less oxygen and exhibited reduced reticular mitochondrial morphology (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), strongly suggesting reductions in oxidative phosphorylation (Galloway et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on experimental observations and cited literature.

claim: A transient 69% increase of the ROS byproduct, superoxide, was observed in mitochondria isolated from brain tissue two hours after concussive injury in wild-type mice.
source: Two hours after concussive injury in mice, a transient 69% increase of the ROS byproduct, superoxide, was observed in mitochondria isolated from brain tissue compared to a 6% increase in Surf1-/- mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring mitochondrial superoxide shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A 6% increase in superoxide was observed in mitochondria isolated from Surf1-/- mouse brain tissue two hours after concussive injury.
source: Two hours after concussive injury in mice, a transient 69% increase of the ROS byproduct, superoxide, was observed in mitochondria isolated from brain tissue compared to a 6% increase in Surf1-/- mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring mitochondrial superoxide shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Metabolite analysis from brain homogenates shows a 61% increase in glutathione oxidation within 2 hr of injury in wild-type animals.
source: Moreover, metabolite analysis from brain homogenates shows a 61% increase in glutathione oxidation within 2 hr of injury in wild-type animals, which was not observed in Surf1-/- mutants (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite analysis data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Increased glutathione oxidation within 2 hr of injury was not observed in Surf1-/- mutants.
source: Moreover, metabolite analysis from brain homogenates shows a 61% increase in glutathione oxidation within 2 hr of injury in wild-type animals, which was not observed in Surf1-/- mutants (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolite analysis data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Decreased cytochrome C oxidase activity suppresses transient trauma-induced ROS accumulation, a process conserved from worm to mouse.
source: Thus, decreased cytochrome C oxidase activity suppresses transient trauma-induced ROS accumulation, a process conserved from worm to mouse.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental data in both C. elegans and mice models.

claim: The basal mitochondrial superoxide levels and oxidized glutathione were significantly elevated in the Surf1-/- brains compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Notably, the basal mitochondrial superoxide levels and oxidized glutathione were significantly elevated in the Surf1-/- brains compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Minimizing transient production and accumulation of oxidative species immediately after trauma parallels neuroprotection.
source: Therefore, minimizing transient production and accumulation of oxidative species immediately after trauma parallels neuroprotection.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the correlation between reduced ROS and neuroprotection.

claim: Traumatic brain injury is a costly energetic process in which neurons work to re-establish resting membrane potential and facilitate cellular repair.
source: Traumatic brain injury is a costly energetic process in which neurons work to re-establish resting membrane potential and facilitate cellular repair (Giza and Hovda, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on TBI energetics.

claim: ATP levels in the Surf1-/- brain were not affected compared to wild type littermates.
source: Despite the apparent decrease in oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 4C), ATP levels in the Surf1-/- brain were not affected compared to wild type littermates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data measuring ATP levels shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Respiratory exchange rate, food intake, body temperature, and overall body weight were unaffected in Surf1-/- mice.
source: Furthermore, respiratory exchange rate, food intake, body temperature, and overall body weight were also unaffected in Surf1-/- mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolic cage analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E.

claim: Surf1-/- mice likely accommodate their energetic needs through alternate means in response to suboptimal mitochondrial respiration.
source: Thus, Surf1-/- mice likely accommodate their energetic needs through alternate means in response to suboptimal mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that ATP levels are maintained despite reduced oxidative phosphorylation.

claim: Post-trauma, the brain transiently increases glycolysis.
source: Post-trauma, the brain transiently increases glycolysis (Yoshino et al., 1991) and will readily metabolize the glycolytic by-product, lactate (Glenn et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on post-trauma brain metabolism.

claim: The brain will readily metabolize the glycolytic by-product, lactate, post-trauma.
source: Post-trauma, the brain transiently increases glycolysis (Yoshino et al., 1991) and will readily metabolize the glycolytic by-product, lactate (Glenn et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on lactate metabolism.

claim: Surf1-/- animals appeared to undergo a Warburg-like increase in glycolysis.
source: Surf1-/- animals appeared to undergo this Warburg-like increase in glycolysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on subsequent experimental observations.

claim: Increased blood lactate has been reported in Surf1-/- mice.
source: Consistent with elevated blood lactate reported in Surf1-/- mice (Pulliam et al., 2014), increased transcription of the lactate dehydrogenase, Ldhd, in the Surf1-/- brain correlated with the rapid acidification of growth media by Surf1-/- cells (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on Surf1-/- mouse metabolism.

claim: Increased transcription of the lactate dehydrogenase, Ldhd, in the Surf1-/- brain correlated with the rapid acidification of growth media by Surf1-/- cells.
source: Consistent with elevated blood lactate reported in Surf1-/- mice (Pulliam et al., 2014), increased transcription of the lactate dehydrogenase, Ldhd, in the Surf1-/- brain correlated with the rapid acidification of growth media by Surf1-/- cells (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5A and media acidification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Transcriptional upregulation of the lactate dehydrogenase, ldh-1, was observed in worms treated with cox-5b RNAi.
source: Similar transcriptional upregulation of the lactate dehydrogenase, ldh-1, was also observed in worms treated with cox-5b RNAi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Neuroprotection by reduced cytochrome C oxidase is the result of preconditioning through metabolic reallocation.
source: We hypothesized that neuroprotection by reduced cytochrome C oxidase is the result of preconditioning through metabolic reallocation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: By preemptively shifting metabolism away from mitochondria respiration, the likelihood of overwhelming ETC function is reduced during the metabolic demand of TBI.
source: By preemptively shifting metabolism away from mitochondria respiration, the likelihood of overwhelming ETC function is reduced during the metabolic demand of TBI.
evidence: The claim is a mechanistic explanation based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The brain relies more heavily on normoxic glycolysis in a process referred to as the Warburg effect to accommodate energetic needs.
source: To accommodate energetic needs, the brain relies more heavily on normoxic glycolysis in a process referred to as the Warburg effect (Warburg, 1956).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of the Warburg effect with citation.

claim: Transcriptional upregulation of several enzymes in the glycolytic pathway was observed in Surf1-/- brains.
source: In Surf1-/- brains, we observed transcriptional upregulation of several enzymes in the glycolytic pathway (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) is inactivated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases, PDK1-4, through phosphorylation of its E1 alpha subunit (PDHE1α).
source: As a critical regulator of the Warburg shunt, which facilitates the shift from mitochondrial respiration to cytosolic glycolysis, the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) is inactivated by pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases, PDK1-4, through phosphorylation of its E1 alpha subunit (PDHE1α) (Kolobova et al., 2001; Patel and Korotchkina, 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge with citations.

claim: Transcriptional upregulation of the brain-enriched Pdk2 was observed in the brains of Surf1 mutants.
source: In the brains of Surf1 mutants, we observed transcriptional upregulation of the brain-enriched Pdk2 in conjunction with the repression of its complementary PDH phosphatase, Pdp1 (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Repression of the PDH phosphatase, Pdp1, was observed in the brains of Surf1 mutants.
source: In the brains of Surf1 mutants, we observed transcriptional upregulation of the brain-enriched Pdk2 in conjunction with the repression of its complementary PDH phosphatase, Pdp1 (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: PDHE1α phosphorylation has previously been reported after open-head brain injury.
source: PDHE1α phosphorylation has previously been reported after open-head brain injury and provides a potential molecular explanation for trauma-induced hyperglycolysis (Xing et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on brain injury.

claim: PDHE1α phosphorylation provides a potential molecular explanation for trauma-induced hyperglycolysis.
source: PDHE1α phosphorylation has previously been reported after open-head brain injury and provides a potential molecular explanation for trauma-induced hyperglycolysis (Xing et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on cited literature and biochemical knowledge.

claim: Increased PDHE1α phosphorylation was observed both before and after injury in Surf1-/- compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Consistent with transcriptional changes in Surf1-/- brains, we observed increased PDHE1α phosphorylation both before and after injury in Surf1-/- compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), while total PDH levels are equivalent (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Total PDH levels are equivalent between Surf1-/- and wild-type littermates.
source: Consistent with transcriptional changes in Surf1-/- brains, we observed increased PDHE1α phosphorylation both before and after injury in Surf1-/- compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), while total PDH levels are equivalent (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Surf1 mutants are preconditioned prior to injury into a Warburg-like state, which likely mitigates the transient ROS production observed immediately after concussion.
source: Thus, Surf1 mutants are preconditioned prior to injury into a Warburg-like state, which likely mitigates the transient ROS production observed immediately after concussion.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental observations.

claim: The brain-enriched Warburg shunt regulator, Pdk2, was elevated in astrocytes.
source: Consistent with the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, the brain-enriched Warburg shunt regulator, Pdk2, as well as every activated glycolytic gene except for Gpi1, was elevated in astrocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single nuclei RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Every activated glycolytic gene except for Gpi1 was elevated in astrocytes.
source: Consistent with the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, the brain-enriched Warburg shunt regulator, Pdk2, as well as every activated glycolytic gene except for Gpi1, was elevated in astrocytes (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single nuclei RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Steady-state expression of the PDK2 protein was confined to astrocytes within the midbrain.
source: Indirect immunofluorescence within the midbrain confirmed that steady-state expression of the PDK2 protein was confined to astrocytes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1P and Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1P and Q.

claim: Glycolytic transcripts were elevated within Surf1 mutant astrocytes compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Moreover, glycolytic transcripts were elevated within Surf1 mutant astrocytes compared to wild-type littermates (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by single nuclei RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The neuroprotective Warburg shift initiated by electron transport impairment originates within astrocytes.
source: Through cellular resolution of this glycolytic preconditioning mechanism, we provide evidence that the neuroprotective Warburg shift initiated by electron transport impairment originates within astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the single nuclei RNA sequencing data showing astrocyte-specific changes.

claim: The hypoxia inducible factor, Hif1a, promotes aerobic glycolysis by activating expression of PDK and glycolytic genes.
source: To understand the molecular mechanisms linking the Surf1 mutation with the Warburg effect, we examined the hypoxia inducible factor, Hif1a, which promotes aerobic glycolysis by activating expression of PDK and glycolytic genes (Kim et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on Hif1a function.

claim: Mitochondria act as oxygen sensors which can signal to cytosolic HIF1α through ROS production.
source: Mitochondria act as oxygen sensors which can signal to cytosolic HIF1α through ROS production (Guzy et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on mitochondrial signaling.

claim: Elevated ROS production caused by paraquat treatment was sufficient to stabilize HIF1α in culture.
source: We confirmed that elevated ROS production caused by paraquat treatment was sufficient to stabilize HIF1α in culture (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Elevated basal ROS levels observed in Surf1-/- brains reduce mitochondrial respiration in favor of glycolysis through Hif1a activation.
source: We hypothesized that elevated basal ROS levels observed in Surf1-/- brains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) reduce mitochondrial respiration in favor of glycolysis through Hif1a activation.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on experimental observations.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of trauma-induced Hif1a activation has previously been shown to enhance necrotic lesion formation after brain trauma.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of trauma-induced Hif1a activation has previously been shown to enhance necrotic lesion formation after brain trauma (Umschweif et al., 2013), suggesting a neuroprotective role for Hif1a activation in concussive injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on Hif1a in brain trauma.

claim: Hif1a activation has a neuroprotective role in concussive injury.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of trauma-induced Hif1a activation has previously been shown to enhance necrotic lesion formation after brain trauma (Umschweif et al., 2013), suggesting a neuroprotective role for Hif1a activation in concussive injury.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on cited literature showing that inhibiting Hif1a worsens outcomes.

claim: Reducing cytochrome C oxidase activity through cox-5b RNAi increased hif-1 activity in C. elegans.
source: Consistent with previous studies in C. elegans (Lee et al., 2010), reducing cytochrome C oxidase activity through cox-5b RNAi increased hif-1 activity as evidenced by induction of the established hif-1 transcriptional target in C. elegans, nhr-57 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1L and cited literature.

claim: HIF1α protein stabilization was observed in Surf1-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: Supporting this conserved response, we observed HIF1α protein stabilization in Surf1-/-mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K) as well as transcriptional upregulation of established glycolytic Hif1a targets in Surf1-/- brains, including critical enzymes in the Warburg shunt (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claim: Transcriptional upregulation of established glycolytic Hif1a targets was observed in Surf1-/- brains, including critical enzymes in the Warburg shunt.
source: Supporting this conserved response, we observed HIF1α protein stabilization in Surf1-/-mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K) as well as transcriptional upregulation of established glycolytic Hif1a targets in Surf1-/- brains, including critical enzymes in the Warburg shunt (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mild elevation of ROS caused by reduced ETC function promotes a Hif1a mediated Warburg-like effect in the brain.
source: Our data indicates that mild elevation of ROS caused by reduced ETC function, promotes a Hif1a mediated Warburg-like effect in the brain, which reduces the chance of overwhelming mitochondrial respiratory capacity under the strong energetic demand of TBI.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental observations.

claim: The Hif1a mediated Warburg-like effect reduces the chance of overwhelming mitochondrial respiratory capacity under the strong energetic demand of TBI.
source: Our data indicates that mild elevation of ROS caused by reduced ETC function, promotes a Hif1a mediated Warburg-like effect in the brain, which reduces the chance of overwhelming mitochondrial respiratory capacity under the strong energetic demand of TBI.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental observations.

claim: Administration of dichloroacetate (DCA) resulted in Surf1 mutants no longer being protected against trauma-induced neurodegeneration.
source: To examine the necessity of this Warburg shift in our neuroprotective model, we administered the pharmacological Warburg inhibitor, dichloroacetate (DCA), and observed that Surf1 mutants were no longer protected against trauma-induced neurodegeneration (Figure 5E and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 1R).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DCA treatment shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: pdp-1 expression was repressed in C. elegans after blunt force injury.
source: Consistent with earlier reports of rodent brain injury (Lazzarino et al., 2019) and SURF1 mutants (Figure 5A), pdp-1 expression was repressed in C. elegans after blunt force injury (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptional data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I and cited literature.

claim: pdp-1 RNAi suppressed degeneration of dopaminergic neurons after trauma in C. elegans.
source: To further validate the Warburg shift as a neuroprotective mechanism, we employed genetic means in C. elegans and observed that pdp-1 RNAi suppressed degeneration of dopaminergic neurons after trauma (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Reduced expression of pdp-1 exclusively in the nervous system was sufficient to promote survival of dopaminergic neurons after blunt force trauma.
source: Albeit to a lesser degree, reduced expression of pdp-1 exclusively in the nervous system was sufficient to promote survival of dopaminergic neurons after blunt force trauma (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from tissue-specific RNAi shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Modulating PDC activity through the key regulatory factors is sufficient to suppress trauma-induced neurodegeneration in both mice and worms.
source: Thus, modulating PDC activity through the key regulatory factors is sufficient to suppress trauma-induced neurodegeneration in both mice and worms.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental data in both C. elegans and mice models.

claim: The physiological properties and regulatory mechanisms inherent to different neuronal subtypes likely determine their vulnerability to trauma.
source: Rather than being a stochastic mechanism of progressive tissue degeneration dictated by the type and site of injury, the physiological properties and regulatory mechanisms inherent to different neuronal subtypes likely determine their vulnerability to trauma.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation of selective dopaminergic vulnerability despite comparable mechanical strain.

claim: Genetic modification of a single gene can suppress degeneration of dopaminergic neurons following concussive injury.
source: Furthermore, these complementary models were used to demonstrate that genetic modification of a single gene can suppress degeneration of this neuronal subtype following concussive injury.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing neuroprotection by Surf1 mutation and cox-5b RNAi.

claim: Pharmacological induction of Parkinsonian phenotypes, including death of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain, requires highly oxidative drugs that irreversibly inhibit mitochondrial ETC complexes I and III.
source: Pharmacological induction of Parkinsonian phenotypes, including death of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain, requires highly oxidative drugs that irreversibly inhibit mitochondrial ETC complexes I and III (Subramaniam and Chesselet, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on Parkinson's disease models.

claim: ETC complex IV insufficiency protects dopaminergic neurons from trauma-induced degeneration.
source: Yet, our studies demonstrate that ETC complex IV insufficiency protects dopaminergic neurons from trauma-induced degeneration.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data from the study.

claim: The neuroprotective effects of ETC complex IV insufficiency are attributed to a metabolic shift away from mitochondrial respiration, which minimizes or even abolishes transient oxidative stress in the neuron and suppresses dopaminergic degeneration.
source: We attribute these neuroprotective effects to a metabolic shift away from mitochondrial respiration, which minimizes or even abolishes transient oxidative stress in the neuron and suppresses dopaminergic degeneration.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental observations.

claim: ROS can have beneficial roles in the cell as a signaling molecule.
source: Although often thought of as unavoidable toxic byproducts of oxidative phosphorylation, ROS can have beneficial roles in the cell as a signaling molecule (Guzy et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on ROS signaling.

claim: Both toxic and protective mechanisms of ROS are operating in the complementary models of blunt force injury.
source: In our complementary models of blunt force injury, we believe that both toxic and protective mechanisms of ROS are operating, which historically has been difficult to discern.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation that basal ROS is elevated in Surf1-/- but transient ROS is protective.

claim: Trauma-induced hyperglycolysis was reported decades ago yet its cellular resolution and pathophysiological role have remained unclear.
source: Trauma-induced hyperglycolysis was reported decades ago yet its cellular resolution and pathophysiological role have remained unclear (Bergsneider et al., 1997; Carpenter et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on trauma-induced hyperglycolysis.

claim: The astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle is a crucial mechanism by which the brain maintains energetic homeostasis.
source: The astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle is a crucial mechanism by which the brain maintains energetic homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Perturbations to the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle system have been reported in neurodegenerative disorders and contribute to disease progression.
source: Perturbations to this system have been reported in neurodegenerative disorders and contribute to disease progression (Mason, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on neurodegenerative disorders.

claim: Preemptively repressing mitochondrial respiration initiates a Warburg-like response in astrocytes as an attempt to restore homeostatic energetics.
source: Our data suggests that preemptively repressing mitochondrial respiration initiates a Warburg-like response in astrocytes as an attempt to restore homeostatic energetics.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The injured brain likely induces hyperglycolysis in astrocytes as a protective mechanism to mitigate the oxidative damage resulting from over-activated mitochondrial respiration.
source: Thus, the injured brain likely induces hyperglycolysis in astrocytes as a protective mechanism to mitigate the oxidative damage resulting from over-activated mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Cerebral metabolic preconditioning presents a plausible prophylactic method for individuals at higher risk for TBI.
source: Cerebral metabolic preconditioning presents a plausible prophylactic method for individuals at higher risk for TBI.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the study findings.

claim: Neuroinflammation does not correlate with the rapid emergence of dopaminergic neurodegeneration in this study.
source: Interestingly, neuroinflammation does not correlate with the rapid emergence of dopaminergic neurodegeneration in our study.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental observations showing no neuroinflammation.

claim: Neuroinflammation and other factors likely contribute to the later stages of this neurodegenerative condition.
source: However, neuroinflammation and other factors likely contribute to the later stages of this neurodegenerative condition (McKee et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on cited literature and inference.

claim: Longitudinal studies are required to further characterize disease progression, including neuroinflammation and proteotoxicity, after the initial loss of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain.
source: Therefore, longitudinal studies are required to further characterize disease progression, including neuroinflammation and proteotoxicity, after the initial loss of dopaminergic neurons in the midbrain.
evidence: The claim is a recommendation for future research based on the study's limitations.

claim: The adult nematode, C. elegans, possesses 302 post-mitotic neurons.
source: In contrast to the cellular and network complexity of the human brain, the adult nematode, C. elegans, possesses 302 post-mitotic neurons (White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge with citation.

claim: Concussion is associated with a myriad of deleterious immediate and long-term consequences.
source: Concussion is associated with a myriad of deleterious immediate and long-term consequences.
evidence: The claim is based on established medical knowledge.

claim: The molecular mechanisms and genetic targets promoting the selective vulnerability of different neural subtypes to dysfunction and degeneration remain unclear.
source: Yet the molecular mechanisms and genetic targets promoting the selective vulnerability of different neural subtypes to dysfunction and degeneration remain unclear.
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Reduction of mitochondrial electron flux through complex IV suppresses trauma-induced degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in a conserved manner between C. elegans and mice.
source: Translating experimental models of blunt force trauma in C. elegans to concussion in mice, we identify a conserved neuroprotective mechanism in which reduction of mitochondrial electron flux through complex IV suppresses trauma-induced degeneration of the highly vulnerable dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data from both model organisms.

claim: Reducing cytochrome C oxidase function elevates mitochondrial-derived reactive oxygen species.
source: Reducing cytochrome C oxidase function elevates mitochondrial-derived reactive oxygen species, which signal through the cytosolic hypoxia inducing transcription factor, Hif1a, to promote hyperphosphorylation and inactivation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase, PDHE1α.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing elevated basal ROS in Surf1-/- brains.

claim: Mitochondrial-derived reactive oxygen species signal through the cytosolic hypoxia inducing transcription factor, Hif1a, to promote hyperphosphorylation and inactivation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase, PDHE1α.
source: Reducing cytochrome C oxidase function elevates mitochondrial-derived reactive oxygen species, which signal through the cytosolic hypoxia inducing transcription factor, Hif1a, to promote hyperphosphorylation and inactivation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase, PDHE1α.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing HIF1α stabilization and PDHE1α phosphorylation.

claim: PDHE1α initiates the Warburg shunt, which drives energetic reallocation from mitochondrial respiration to astrocyte-mediated glycolysis in a neuroprotective manner.
source: This critical enzyme initiates the Warburg shunt, which drives energetic reallocation from mitochondrial respiration to astrocyte-mediated glycolysis in a neuroprotective manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing glycolytic upregulation in astrocytes and neuroprotection.

claim: Glycolytic preconditioning suppresses Parkinson-like hypersensitivity of dopaminergic neurons to trauma-induced degeneration via redox signaling and the Warburg effect.
source: These studies demonstrate a conserved process in which glycolytic preconditioning suppresses Parkinson-like hypersensitivity of dopaminergic neurons to trauma-induced degeneration via redox signaling and the Warburg effect.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the combined experimental observations.

claim: Selective vulnerability of different neuronal subtypes to dysfunction, degeneration, and death underlies all neurological diseases.
source: Selective vulnerability of different neuronal subtypes to dysfunction, degeneration, and death underlies all neurological diseases.
evidence: The claim is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Differential interplay between genetic and environmental factors contribute to neuronal selectivity.
source: Differential interplay between genetic and environmental factors contribute to this neuronal selectivity.
evidence: The claim is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Environmental stimuli have the capacity to trigger pathogenic cascades contingent on genetic factors.
source: Environmental stimuli have the capacity to trigger pathogenic cascades contingent on genetic factors.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of gene-environment interactions.

claim: The initial biomechanical insult of TBI precipitates numerous cellular and systemic alterations with the potential to promote neurological dysfunction and progressive neurodegeneration.
source: Such is the case for traumatic brain injury (TBI) and concussion, in which the initial biomechanical insult precipitates numerous cellular and systemic alterations with the potential to promote neurological dysfunction and progressive neurodegeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of TBI pathophysiology.

claim: Ionic imbalances, cytoskeletal disruption, aberrant proteostasis, genomic instability, and mitochondrial dysfunction within neurons and support cells initiate systemic abnormalities after TBI.
source: In particular, ionic imbalances, cytoskeletal disruption, aberrant proteostasis, genomic instability, and mitochondrial dysfunction within neurons and support cells initiate systemic abnormalities including metabolic impairment, vascular disruption, inflammation, blood-brain barrier defects, and reduced cerebral blood-flow (Giza et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on TBI pathophysiology.

claim: The stochastic nature of the mechanical insult has complicated our ability to define the underlying mechanisms of neurodegeneration.
source: Yet, the stochastic nature of the mechanical insult has complicated our ability to define the underlying mechanisms of neurodegeneration.
evidence: The claim identifies a challenge in the field.

claim: It remains unclear whether the inherent chemical properties of different neuronal subtypes confer varying degrees of vulnerability to trauma-induced neurodegeneration.
source: It remains unclear whether the inherent chemical properties of different neuronal subtypes confer varying degrees of vulnerability to trauma-induced neurodegeneration.
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The genetic contribution to TBI is poorly understood.
source: Additionally, the genetic contribution to this widespread disorder is poorly understood, genetic effectors are likely to amplify the cellular and systemic aberrations initiated by the mechanical insult.
evidence: The claim identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Genetic effectors are likely to amplify the cellular and systemic aberrations initiated by the mechanical insult of TBI.
source: Additionally, the genetic contribution to this widespread disorder is poorly understood, genetic effectors are likely to amplify the cellular and systemic aberrations initiated by the mechanical insult.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on general principles of gene-environment interactions.

claim: Genetic targeting and modulation may be sufficient to suppress the ensuing neurodegeneration after concussive brain injury.
source: Thereby, we hypothesize that genetic targeting and modulation may be sufficient to suppress the ensuing neurodegeneration after concussive brain injury.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Metabolic fluctuations in the brain occurring with age or injury have been linked with neurological health.
source: Metabolic fluctuations in the brain occurring with age or injury have been linked with neurological health (Camandola and Mattson, 2017; Marino et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on brain metabolism and health.

claim: The neurometabolic cascade resulting from concussion is characterized by erratic fluctuations in metabolism.
source: The neurometabolic cascade resulting from concussion is characterized by erratic fluctuations in metabolism, which are hypothesized to accommodate the energetic demand required for neuronal repolarization and repair (Giza and Hovda, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on concussion metabolism.

claim: Metabolic fluctuations after concussion are hypothesized to accommodate the energetic demand required for neuronal repolarization and repair.
source: The neurometabolic cascade resulting from concussion is characterized by erratic fluctuations in metabolism, which are hypothesized to accommodate the energetic demand required for neuronal repolarization and repair (Giza and Hovda, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing this hypothesis.

claim: Brain energetics relies heavily on mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and cytosolic glycolysis.
source: Brain energetics relies heavily on two metabolic pathways including mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and cytosolic glycolysis (Kasischke et al., 2004; Pellerin and Magistretti, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on brain energetics.

claim: The astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (ANLS) entails astrocytic production and transport of the glycolytic by-product, lactate, to neurons which preferentially oxidize it rather than glucose to meet their energetic demands.
source: The astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle (ANLS) entails astrocytic production and transport of the glycolytic by-product, lactate, to neurons which preferentially oxidize it rather than glucose to meet their energetic demands (Magistretti et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on the ANLS.

claim: Immediately following injury, rodent brains display signs of decreased oxidative phosphorylation that can persist for weeks.
source: Immediately following injury, rodent brains display signs of decreased oxidative phosphorylation that can persist for weeks (Gilmer et al., 2009; Xiong et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on post-injury brain metabolism.

claim: The injured brain transiently elevates normoxic glycolysis in humans and animal models.
source: Conversely, the injured brain transiently elevates normoxic glycolysis in humans and animal models (Bergsneider et al., 1997; Sokoloff et al., 1977; Yoshino et al., 1991), suggesting an energetic reallocation through astrocytic means.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on post-injury glycolysis.

claim: Transient elevation of normoxic glycolysis after brain injury suggests an energetic reallocation through astrocytic means.
source: Conversely, the injured brain transiently elevates normoxic glycolysis in humans and animal models (Bergsneider et al., 1997; Sokoloff et al., 1977; Yoshino et al., 1991), suggesting an energetic reallocation through astrocytic means.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on cited literature and knowledge of the ANLS.

claim: The Warburg effect is a phenomena observed in cancer cells in which aerobic glycolysis is favored over oxidative phosphorylation.
source: This metabolic shift is a phenomena observed in cancer cells and is termed the Warburg effect, in which aerobic glycolysis is favored over oxidative phosphorylation (Warburg, 1956).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge with citation.

claim: The injured brain initially undergoes a Warburg-like response.
source: Thus, the injured brain initially undergoes a Warburg-like response, but how this metabolic shift occurs within the astrocyte-neuron axis and its ability to impact neurological function and degeneration after concussion is not well understood.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cited literature showing increased glycolysis after injury.
